newsitem.title: CHINA: Income gap widens between China urban, rural areas.
newsitem.headline: Income gap widens between China urban, rural areas.

text.p: China's urban residents have become richer while their rural cousins have fallen behind in the two decades after late paramount leader Deng Xiaoping freed people to make money, officials said on Tuesday.

The gap between provinces along the east coast and those in the western hinterland had widened since China abandoned Soviet-style central planning in the late 1970s, Xian Zude, deputy director of the State Statistical Bureau's department of agriculture, told a news conference.
However, the gap between rich and poor as well as east and west was "reasonable" and not a cause for social instability, Xian said.
"It is inevitable for discrepancies to widen at a stage when the economy is taking off," Xian said.

About 80 percent of China's 1.2 billion people live in rural areas, and while their incomes have soared since Deng told his people that "to get rich is glorious" they have far to go to catch up with their urban cousins.
Xian attributed the widening gap in part to preferential policies the government gives to coastal provinces as well as to cheap raw materials provided by western regions to the east.
The income gap between urban and rural residents was wider in areas where the economy was still struggling and narrower in regions where the economy was booming, he said.
Farmers in their top 20 percent income bracket earned only the equivalent of urban residents in the second 20 percent.
Urban per capita income in the first half of this year rose by an inflation-adjusted 2.2 percent to 2,680 yuan ($322) while per capita income was just 980 yuan, up a real 3.3 percent.
Consumption was also higher in urban areas, where residents ate an average of 20 kg of meat and 9.7 kg of eggs a year compared with 11 kg and 3.2 kg respectively in rural areas.
In urban areas, 89 percent of families owned washing machines compared with 17 percent in rural areas while 66 percent had refrigerators against just five percent of farmers.

Black and white television sets were the sole exception with more rural families owning such household appliances than urban families -- 64 percent of rural families compared with 39 percent in cities, Xian said.
"The rural market is 10-15 years behind the urban market in terms of consumption," he said.

Farmers in eastern China earned more than their counterparts in inland western regions. In 1996, per capita income of farmers in eastern China was 2,558 yuan compared with 1,290 yuan in western regions, Xian said without giving comparative figures.

The top earners are farmers from Shanghai, Beijing and the coastal provinces of Zhejiang, Guangdong and Jiangsu, while the poorest were from the hinterland -- western Gansu, Shaanxi, Qinghai and southwestern Yunnan and Guizhou, he said.
The annual per capita income of farmers in Shanghai was about 4,800 yuan compared with 1,100 yuan in the northwestern province of Gansu, Xian said.

The government was torn between "giving priority to efficiency and giving consideration to justice", Xian said in reference the paradox in socialist China of rapid economic development versus equal distribution of wealth.
It has tried to narrow the gap pouring billions of yuan into a fund to aid the impoverished, he said.
China had 58 million destitute people by the end of 1996, half living in northwest and southwest regions.
